lesson.title: Temperature, colour and motion

steps.headline: A hotter star peaks at a shorter wavelength: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ T.

lead.text: A star radiates roughly like a blackbody, whose spectrum has a single peak. Wien's law gives the peak wavelength from the surface temperature T in kelvin. Hotter means a shorter peak, so bluer light.

steps.headline: Find the peak wavelength of a star with a surface temperature of 9,000 K.

workedSteps.text: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
Convert metres to nanometres by multiplying by 10⁹.
Compare with visible light, which runs from about 400 to 700 nm.

lead.text: Same law, with the Sun's surface temperature. Give the peak in nanometres.

reveal.text: The Sun's peak is in the blue-green, but it emits right across the visible range, so it looks white.

lead.text: Run Wien's law backwards to take a star's temperature from a distance: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K ÷ λmax. Write λmax in metres.

reveal.text: A peak at 290 nm lies in the ultraviolet. Hot stars like Vega, near 10,000 K, look blue-white.

steps.headline: A receding source's light shifts to longer wavelengths, by v = cΔλ/λ.

lead.text: Laboratory wavelengths are fixed. A source moving away stretches its waves: a redshift. One approaching squeezes them: a blueshift. For speeds well below light's, the speed along the line of sight is v = cΔλ/λ.
Δλ is the observed wavelength minus the laboratory one. Positive means receding.

reveal.text: A shift of about 1% of the wavelength means a speed of about 1% of c. That is how astronomers measure speeds of stars and galaxies they will never visit.

lead.text: Stars in our galaxy move at tens to hundreds of kilometres per second, so their shifts are tiny. An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.

reveal.text: The line moves 0.25 nm towards the blue. Only motion along the line of sight shows up: sideways motion produces no first-order shift.

lesson.orientation: Read a star's temperature from its colour and its motion from shifted spectral lines.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Atoms emit light at fixed wavelengths. When the source moves away from you, the waves it sends are stretched.

intro.promise: By the end you'll read a star's temperature from its colour and its speed from the shift in its spectral lines.

recap.keyIdea: A star's colour gives its temperature through Wien's law, and the shift of its spectral lines gives its speed along our line of sight, v = cΔλ/λ.

blocks.text: You found that the Sun peaks at 502 nm, that a 290 nm peak means about 10,000 K, and that a 1% stretch of a line means a speed of 1% of light's.

recap.nextHook: Temperature and brightness are two measurements of a star. What happens when you plot one against the other?

questions.prompt: Using Wien's law λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T, find the peak wavelength of the Sun (T = 5,772 K) in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Divide Wien's constant by the temperature.
The result comes out in metres.
Multiply by 10⁹ to convert metres to nanometres.
questions.onCorrect: 502 nm. Wien's law gives metres; multiply by 10⁹ to get nanometres.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres. Multiply by 10⁹ to turn it into nanometres.

questions.prompt: A star's spectrum peaks at 290 nm. Find its surface temperature in kelvin, to the nearest hundred.
hints: Rearrange Wien's law for T.
Write the peak wavelength in metres.
Divide the constant by that wavelength, then round.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: T = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 2.90 × 10⁻⁷ = 9,993 K, which is 10,000 K to the nearest hundred.

questions.onCorrect: 10,000 K. Divide the constant by the peak wavelength in metres, then round.

misconceptions.feedback: Round your answer to the nearest hundred, as the question asks.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line with laboratory wavelength 656.28 nm is observed at 662.84 nm. Using v = cΔλ/λ with c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s, find the radial velocity in km/s, to the nearest ten (positive means receding).
hints: Find the shift: observed minus laboratory wavelength.
Divide the shift by the laboratory wavelength.
Multiply by the speed of light in km/s.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Δλ = 6.56 nm; v = 3.00 × 10⁵ × 6.56/656.28 = 2,999 km/s, which is 3,000 km/s to the nearest ten, receding.

questions.onCorrect: 3,000 km/s receding. Shift ÷ laboratory wavelength × c gives the speed.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the shift in nanometres. Divide by the laboratory wavelength, then multiply by c.
The line moved to a longer wavelength. That is a redshift, so the velocity is positive.

questions.prompt: A star approaches at 150 km/s. Find the shift of its 500.00 nm line in nanometres, with redshift positive and blueshift negative, to three decimal places. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.
hints: An approaching source has a negative radial velocity.
Use Δλ = λv/c.
Multiply 500 by −150, then divide by 300,000.
questions.onCorrect: −0.25 nm. An approaching star has negative velocity, so its lines shift towards the blue.

misconceptions.feedback: The star is approaching, so the line moves to shorter wavelengths. That makes the shift negative.

questions.prompt: Betelgeuse looks orange-red and Rigel looks blue-white. What does the difference tell you?
hints: Which property of a glowing body sets where its spectrum peaks?

acceptedIdeas: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: about 3,600 K for Betelgeuse against about 12,000 K for Rigel. Their radial speeds are far too small to change a colour.

choices.label: Betelgeuse's surface is cooler, so its spectrum peaks at longer wavelengths
Betelgeuse is moving away from us much faster than Rigel
Betelgeuse is farther away, so its light has reddened on the way

questions.onCorrect: Colour tracks surface temperature through Wien's law: orange-red is cooler, blue-white hotter.

misconceptions.feedback: A speed of a few km/s shifts a line by a tiny fraction. It cannot change a star's colour.
These bright stars are near enough that reddening on the way is small. The colour is set at the surface.

questions.prompt: A red dwarf has a surface temperature of 3,000 K. Find its peak wavelength in nanometres, to the nearest whole number.
hints: Use λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ m·K / T.
Divide by 3,000 K.
Convert metres to nanometres.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: λmax = 2.898 × 10⁻³ / 3,000 = 9.66 × 10⁻⁷ m = 966 nm, in the near infrared.

questions.onCorrect: 966 nm, in the near infrared. A cool star peaks at long wavelengths.

misconceptions.feedback: That is in metres. Multiply by 10⁹ to turn it into nanometres.

questions.prompt: A hydrogen line measures 500 nm in the laboratory and arrives at 505 nm. By what percentage has its wavelength grown?
hints: How many nanometres did the wavelength grow?
Compare that growth with the original wavelength.
Divide the growth by 500, then write it as a percentage.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: The wavelength grew by 5 nm out of 500 nm: 5 ÷ 500 = 0.01, or 1%.

questions.onCorrect: 1%. The stretch is a fraction of the original wavelength, which is what the Doppler shift measures.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the growth in nanometres. A percentage compares the growth with the original wavelength.
That is the fraction. The question asks for a percentage.

questions.prompt: Which star has the shorter peak wavelength?
hints: Look at where T sits in Wien's law.
questions.onCorrect: T is in the denominator, so a hotter star has a smaller λmax and looks bluer.

misconceptions.feedback: A cooler star has a larger λmax, so it peaks at longer wavelengths.
The peak depends on temperature, so different temperatures give different peaks.

questions.prompt: Why does a hotter star have a shorter peak wavelength?
hints: Look at where T sits in the formula.

acceptedIdeas: Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller result.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller result.

choices.label: Wien's law divides by T, so a larger T gives a smaller result.

questions.onCorrect: The constant is divided by T, so raising T lowers λmax.

misconceptions.feedback: Size does not enter Wien's law. Only the temperature does.
Distance does not change a star's peak wavelength. Only the temperature does.

questions.prompt: A star is approaching us. How are its spectral lines shifted?
hints: An approaching source squeezes its waves.
questions.onCorrect: An approaching source squeezes its waves: its lines move towards the blue, a blueshift.

misconceptions.feedback: That is a redshift, which comes from a receding source.
Motion along the line of sight shifts the lines, even if the shift is small.

questions.prompt: A star's hydrogen line, 656.28 nm in the laboratory, is shifted by 1.31 nm. How fast is the star moving along the line of sight, in km/s, to the nearest ten? Use c = 3.00 × 10⁵ km/s.
hints: Divide the shift by the laboratory wavelength.
That fraction is v/c.
Multiply by c in km/s, then round to the nearest ten.
questions.onCorrect: 600 km/s. The shift as a fraction of the wavelength equals the speed as a fraction of c.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the fraction v/c. Multiply by c to get the speed in km/s.
